baer-heitev.1#א: To rely. Explanation: to buy from him; but they rely on him when he says regarding others that it is permitted, as the Mechaber wrote in seif 7. Shach:
baer-heitev.1#ב: Regarding prohibition. Shach wrote: some say other prohibitions that are literally of the Torah; but even wine — stam yeinam is only d'rabbanan, for they decreed upon it lest it be definite libation wine; and some say not only wine but even other matters where there is concern of prohibition that are entirely d'rabbanan, such as cheese and bread of gentiles in a place where they practice prohibition, and the like; and from the conclusion of the Rav's words it appears the same applies to milk — one does not buy from him unless he has a presumption of kosher status. And even though the Mechaber also wrote in siman 65 that one does not buy meat from any butcher who slaughters for himself and sells unless he had a presumption of kosher status — one must say a slaughtering butcher is different, for it is very common and the laws of slaughter are numerous and he can easily cause delay, pressing, or other disqualifications; and if he did not have a presumption of kosher status it is forbidden. But according to Rama in truth there is no distinction, and if one dines with him — the Rav's view is that even l'chatchila one may eat with him.
baer-heitev.2#_: Suspected. Shach wrote: he is not called suspected regarding that matter until he transgresses not for appetite — such as if forbidden and permitted were placed before him he would eat the forbidden; and some say regarding a habitual sinner who eats nevelah for appetite, it is forbidden to eat from his slaughter until he checks the knife for him, as written in siman 2, because knives are often nicked — therefore we are concerned he will transgress for appetite and not trouble to fix it. But here it deals with a matter where there is no concern he will now transgress for appetite; therefore he is not called suspected. Taz wrote: if he is so suspected that even when permitted food is before him he abandons it and eats forbidden — he is like a full gentile; therefore he wrote this Rama gloss has no explanation at all, see there. And Darkei Moshe wrote in the name of Hagahot Asheri that one suspected of a prohibition such that it is forbidden to eat with him — even permitted things, lest he feed him forbidden things as well, end of his words.
baer-heitev.3#א: Substitute. Shach wrote: only for selling he instructs permissibility, but to steal and substitute by hand he is not suspected. And that which appears in siman 118 seif 1 that one does not deposit with a suspected Israelite a d'oraisa forbidden item except with two seals and a d'rabbanan forbidden item with one seal — there it deals with one suspected to substitute, and they abbreviated there because I did not descend to explain there who is called suspected.
baer-heitev.3#ב: Ashamed. Shach wrote: from Rashba it appears where it is known she is not ashamed of the guest as is the way of an innkeeper today who cares nothing about the guest's food — it is permitted. But Tosafot explained the opposite — that she takes the good and gives the guest the bad because she toiled for him; accordingly where he pays her wages for trouble it is possible it is permitted, as Tosafot wrote regarding an agent: if one gives him wages he cannot impose an oath on him, for then he no longer instructs permissibility; and even for Rambam, from whose words it appears that even when one gives wages he can impose an oath because nevertheless he instructs permissibility lest he did not pay his wages properly — it is possible he concedes here regarding an innkeeper's wages.
baer-heitev.4#_: Others. Bach wrote: a butcher suspected regarding milk is suspected regarding all prohibitions — meaning even regarding a matter more severe than milk, see there, for a matter the public are not lenient about. Shach challenged him, for he learned this from Rashba's words, and there it only appears regarding one suspected for a matter the public are not lenient about — he is suspected for that matter to substitute, but not for another matter.
baer-heitev.5#_: They are careful. Shach wrote: perhaps the Mechaber's view is that everything depends on what people are careful about; but where in people's eyes both are equal, we follow the lighter in penalty and the severe in penalty — requires study. Nevertheless all this only deals with one suspected regarding a severe matter, whether in penalty or in people's eyes, who is suspected regarding a lighter matter than it if they are one type of prohibition, such as both being food matters and the like; if not so, no (for a habitual sinner for one matter is not a habitual sinner for the entire Torah except Shabbat and idolatry — see Taz). And so from the Mechaber's words in siman 2 who wrote that a habitual sinner regarding circumcision is not a habitual sinner regarding slaughter; and in the Perishah he wrote he is not suspected regarding a lighter matter unless he has benefit from it — Shach wrote on this that this is not compelling, see there.
baer-heitev.6#_: Both of them. And it appears that even regarding two types of prohibitions, if he returned and was suspected afterward regarding one of them — even the lighter — he is suspected regarding the more severe because he was suspected initially regarding both. Shach.
baer-heitev.7#א: Regarding idolatry. Shach wrote: know that a habitual sinner for libation of wine is also a habitual sinner for the entire Torah.
baer-heitev.7#ב: In other matters. Even regarding his own, even to sell, and likewise to eat with him — only regarding prohibition we say so; but regarding monetary matters, one suspected regarding one matter is disqualified to testify regarding another matter even regarding others', as written in Choshen Mishpat siman 34. And some say that here and in siman 124 seif 9 the Rav ruled anonymously like the Mechaber; and in Choshen Mishpat siman 34 s.k. 205 and in Even HaEzer end of seif 42 the Rav wrote that one suspected regarding sexual immorality is disqualified for testimony about a woman — there the reason is he has an interest in the testimony, for it is pleasing to him that she be available to him frequently, or that she not be available and stolen waters are sweet, etc.; see above siman 127 in the gloss. However all this is regarding a suspected person; but regarding a habitual sinner, meaning one who is established — I wrote above siman 2 and below siman 127 that he is not believed regarding that matter regarding others', end of his words Shach.
baer-heitev.7#ג: Believed. Shach wrote: one may say this is what the Rav meant: one suspected regarding a matter that does not appear to people as a transgression is not called suspected that he should not be believed even under oath; however regarding that matter he is not believed without an oath — and so from the Rav's responsum in siman 124, see there.
baer-heitev.7#ד: Others. Shach wrote: certainly "before the blind do not place a stumbling block" he did not transgress; and this is specifically when others know he practices prohibition in the matter. And some say: behold the Rav wrote in siman 112 seif 15 that one who is careful with gentile bread and eats with others who are not careful — he may eat with them because of hatred; and likewise he may eat with them, for it is different there because bread is the main part of the meal — they permitted him because of hatred since its prohibition is not stringent, as the Rav wrote there. In the responsum of Maharar Levi ibn Chaviv siman 121 he greatly elaborated these laws, and I saw fit to clarify briefly the content and distinctions emerging from his responsum: one who practices prohibition in some matter because he holds the law is so and eats in the house of one who permits it — if the prohibition is recognizable to the one who forbids, the feeder may feed him, for if he did not hold so he would not eat; but when the prohibition is not recognizable it is forbidden, and forbidden to cook for him in his vessels even if they are not ben yomo; and all the more forbidden for the forbearer to tell the permitter to cook for him in vessels that are not ben yomo; but when the permitter cooks l'chatchila for him and for others' need it is also permitted, for it is b'dieved. One who forbids a matter because of ancestral custom and people of his province who practice so — forbidden for the permitter to feed him even if the prohibition is recognizable, just as it is forbidden d'rabbanan to hand a cup of wine to a nazir even though the nazir could take it himself, see above siman 151 seif 1. The forbearer may cook l'chatchila in the permitter's vessels that are not ben yomo or in plain vessels, for we also establish they are not ben yomo since they did not accept the custom to be so stringent; and if the vessel owner is before us we must ask him if he is ben yomo or not; and if the vessel owner is suspected we need not ask; but if he said so himself or they asked and he answered, we rely on him whether ben yomo or not, see above siman 122. All this regards the vessel; but the forbearer is forbidden to eat from the permitter's cooking if he is suspected based on his words that there is no prohibition in it, if the dish is from something customarily containing that fat; but if he is not certainly suspected, only a plain ignoramus — the forbearer may lodge with him even if he is not wise and expert in laws, if he knows the eater forbids that food, whether because of custom or because he holds the law is so. All this is in general; but if there is a custom they act according to their custom — such as in Rhine provinces some places practice prohibition on stomach-milk, and when they come to places that practice leniency they eat from their cooking from the sauce or from meat cooked with the prohibition, and all the more they use their vessels which are ben yomo; specifically when the custom is in food, such as those places practicing prohibition being in the same province that practices leniency and their custom is to eat from their cooking; but if the custom is only in the feeder alone it is not a custom; therefore one from Poland or the like without that custom, when he comes to places practicing leniency — even though they feed neighboring places that practice prohibition — it is forbidden for him to eat from their cooking. However that which it is forbidden to eat something forbidden because of ancestral custom and people of his province — specifically when he does not see leniency in the matter; but when he sees leniency in the matter and comes from a place that practiced prohibition to a place that practiced leniency, he may eat; and it appears even if he intends to return to a place that practices prohibition, since it appears to him it is permitted, see above end of seif R' Yehuda David, end of his words.
baer-heitev.8#_: Under oath. The reason: since he is already suspected regarding the oath to transgress, for he is under oath from Sinai; and even though the oath from Sinai is for a past transgression, since he is under oath and also transgressed a sin he is worse still; and further there is no distinction between a future oath or a past oath except regarding monetary matters, but not regarding prohibition — see Choshen Mishpat siman 92 seif 2 and siman 87 seif 15. And it appears all the more he is not believed regarding a lighter matter than it under oath. Maharshal wrote: nevertheless one suspected regarding stam yeinam as in these generations may be believed regarding yayin nesech when he swears on it, only they should specify the oath well that he is not under oath from Sinai, because he is lenient regarding stam yeinam which is d'rabbanan, end of his words; and he wrote he so ruled in practice; and perhaps he did not rule so except regarding stam yeinam because people are lenient about it, but one should not rule so regarding other d'rabbanan prohibitions; and even regarding cheese one should not believe one suspected about it even under oath, for even regarding d'rabbanan prohibitions one may say he is under oath from Sinai for the prohibition "do not turn aside," end of his words Shach.
baer-heitev.11#_: Libation. Shach wrote: the matter is plain that for all prohibitions he is not believed; only he does not make yayin nesech since he is truly a Jew; but regarding reliability in prohibitions, since in any case he worships idols for desire, plainly he is not believed.
baer-heitev.13#א: The money. Because of penalty — Rashi; and accordingly it appears specifically when it is known he knew they were forbidden things and sold them intentionally we penalize him; if not, no, for perhaps he was inadvertent (and one does not penalize for what he already ate — only that he need not pay except the value of tereifah cheaply; but what remains intact is mistaken transaction and he returns it and the buyer returns the money). And even though explained in seif 17 that a butcher has no excuse to say he was inadvertent — that is regarding prohibition but not to extract money, end of his words Shach. And Taz wrote it appears that even if the prohibition is safek tereifah — what he ate he ate and he returns the money and they did not consider his eating as benefit at all (and Nachalat Binyamin disagrees, for in safek tereifah even if the seller knew it was safek tereifah he does not return money when eaten; and so in Semak Choshen Mishpat siman 234; and what Taz brings from Bechorot is not proof, for there regarding prohibitions of benefit specifically we say so, or regarding a firstborn because he transgressed a rabbinic enactment, see there).
baer-heitev.13#ב: He shall pay. Since he did not cause him prohibition. Rashi.
baer-heitev.13#ג: Returns. The reason: Semak wrote in Choshen Mishpat that siman regarding d'rabbanan prohibition his eating is considered benefit; and Shach wrote the reason: regarding money they established it on Torah law and did not decree prohibition in order to extract money, end of his words.
baer-heitev.14#א: Scribes. And that which is stated in siman 39 seif 2 that if the lung was not checked it is kosher — that is only if it happened once through coercion or inadvertence; but that one who does not know how to check stands and checks intentionally and they ate based on his checking — certainly forbidden by law; and even though this checking is only of their words, for it is like the case of not nullifying prohibition l'chatchila — if they nullified intentionally it is forbidden; and so the Mechaber in siman 99 seif 6, end of his words Shach. And Taz wrote: and even though regarding a butcher we say in Choshen Mishpat siman 306 he is exempt to pay in this law that it is forbidden because of doubt — it is different there because you come to obligate him for his act; therefore one only obligates him for certainty and not doubt; unlike here between seller and buyer, even if the matter is doubt it is mistaken transaction and he would not have given money accordingly — therefore he returns his money. And in Beit Yosef he wrote in the name of Achai: an incident occurred with a needle found in the lung inside the meat after cutting and they forbade the animal, and what he sold and received money he does not return, because the prohibition is not certain but only because of doubt they forbade the animal since it cannot be checked by blowing, and regarding money the burden of proof is on the claimant, end of his words. Behold they compared this law to the butcher case I mentioned, and this is certainly not according to what I wrote above that even in doubt he must return money; nevertheless they judged well, for perhaps it deals with when they ate the meat before it became known it was tereifah, and in this there is no penalty to return money; or even if not yet eaten, perhaps the needle was swallowed before the buyer bought it (meaning regarding the seller who sold the whole animal to the butcher he returns money — investigate) lest it swallowed afterward, as Choshen Mishpat siman 232 seif 11: if within three days he bought, the claimant must bring proof; but if clear it was done with the seller's permission, such as after slaughter he sold to him — clearly mistaken transaction and he returns his money as long as he did not eat the meat; and if he ate, the selling butcher is exempt even though doubt d'oraisa prohibition — nevertheless no penalty applies since he himself did not know; unlike mistaken transaction, as long as meat remains it does not help him that he did not know, for whatever is because of a defect he must return even though he too benefited — plain in Choshen Mishpat siman 232 seif 18 in the gloss. But in truth if the seller knew this doubt and sold to him — certainly even if the buyer ate he returns his money, unlike Levush, see there, end of his words.
baer-heitev.14#ב: From an animal. Taz wrote: even though Shulchan Aruch wrote that if tereifah came because the lung was not checked properly we say if she ate the seller deducts and does not return — nevertheless that is only regarding something that d'oraisa does not require checking when there is no defect; but if there is a defect it automatically requires checking even d'oraisa, and the event occurred that they cannot check — even if the buyer ate the seller must return, for behold he sold doubt d'oraisa prohibition; and this is specifically if the seller knew the doubt, for then penalty applies; if he did not know, he does not return except when not eaten, from mistaken transaction. But Shach disagrees and wrote: since it is doubt, why should the seller return money if already eaten; if the buyer wants to say you have no greater defect than this, the seller says return my sale and I will return your money; now that he ate the seller says who can tell you that you ate tereifah — and so in Semak Choshen Mishpat siman 234 s.k. 1 regarding safek tereifah if eaten he need not return money; rather this is the explanation of Rama's words here: from an animal not checked properly which is certainly forbidden by their words — plainly he must return money while meat exists; but even if he sold something from an animal in which a defect arose requiring forbidding out of doubt, and the seller might say perhaps it is not tereifah and he will bring proof it is tereifah and return money — nevertheless it is as if certainly tereifah by their words and he must return money while meat still exists; and any safek tereifot voids the transaction if meat still exists; but if he already ate the meat the seller need not return anything, end of his words.
baer-heitev.15#_: He shall go. Maharshal wrote: if the sages see he cannot exile from his place because dependents hang on him and his daughter's troubles or the like — they give him repentance in his place with enough restriction to stand in this balance. He also wrote that for one transgression they consider him a stumbling block and should warn him not to do so again. And nevertheless it appears one should forbid vessels retroactively whenever there is doubt even the first time. Shach wrote that even the first time he sold forbidden things they remove him, etc.; and so from the Mechaber seif 17 and what the Rav wrote in Choshen Mishpat siman 306 seif 9: and some say a butcher and teacher even though they do not need warning, nevertheless we require presumption until they are established or permitted — we do not remove them. Ribash already answered: there it deals with only monetary loss and also perhaps they are misled or inadvertent; but one suspected of feeding prohibition — immediately they remove him. Rashba already wrote that a butcher from whom tereifah issued has no excuse to say he was inadvertent, for otherwise he would always say so; and regarding tereifah of vessels see above siman 1. Beit Yosef wrote in Choshen Mishpat siman 34: according to Rambam, if he inspects for himself, since he has monetary benefit, even if he repented he is not restored until he goes where he is not recognized; one who inspects for others, since he has no monetary benefit therein, is restored through repentance.
baer-heitev.16#_: From paying. Since it is only safek tereifot he need not pay the animal's value to the owners, for he can say perhaps it is kosher, and the burden of proof is on the claimant; see Choshen Mishpat siman 306 seif 5. Shach.
baer-heitev.17#_: Excuse. However regarding a person known to be God-fearing and meticulous in his actions — in Mahari Weil's responsum they do not remove him and we say he certainly erred, see there.
baer-heitev.19#א: So-and-so. The reason: he fears lest they ask that so-and-so and he will not lie; and it appears even when the sender did not instruct him to buy from expert so-and-so but he himself says I bought from expert so-and-so — he is believed. Shach.
baer-heitev.19#ב: To substitute. And if you fear perhaps he gives from his own and a person is not apt to give a gift from his own in another's name; and even if he does not mention the expert's name but says a certain expert sent you a gift — he is believed. Shach.
baer-heitev.19#ג: D'oraisa. Taz disagrees with the Rav, for in siman 2 seif 4 regarding a habitual sinner for appetite who said expert so-and-so slaughtered for me — he is believed, and there it is slaughter which is d'oraisa prohibition and nevertheless believed; and another proof from siman 86 we rely on the gentile when he says these eggs are from such-and-so bird, and behold d'oraisa prohibition; and also siman 118 regarding sending a thigh by a gentile cut in the way they cut to remove the gid, etc. — even d'oraisa we apply this reasoning that one does not give from his own in others' names, see there. But Shach answers these difficulties: in siman 2 it deals when we know clearly he did not slaughter — no concern, for most available at slaughter are experts, unlike here; and what we rely on in siman 86 regarding eggs — one may say there since he himself sells to him; but here when he says he bought from another he is not believed in d'oraisa prohibition. However what Taz challenged from siman 118 regarding thigh — Shach did not address this; requires study for practical halachah whether we say this reasoning regarding d'oraisa prohibition.
baer-heitev.20#_: Suspected. Shach wrote the reason: because he is a habitual sinner for that matter but not for other matters — plainly if suspected for one matter he is not suspected for other matters, unlike Bach, see there. And Taz wrote Beit Yosef brought here in the name of Rambam that a suspected person and all the more a gentile is believed regarding others' property to testify that he tithed, for a person does not sin without benefit to himself; and he disagrees, for we establish one suspected regarding a matter is neither judged nor testifies, and so one should rule in practice, end of his words.
